claim: Mendelian diseases affect 6% of the world population.
source: Hereditary diseases affect 6% of the world population and typically lack cure.
evidence: Cited from Ferreira, 2019 as indicated in the text

claim: Hereditary diseases typically lack cure.
source: Hereditary diseases affect 6% of the world population and typically lack cure.
evidence: Cited from Ferreira, 2019 as indicated in the text

claim: Identification of the genetic and molecular basis of hereditary diseases is challenging.
source: Identification of their genetic and molecular basis is challenging, limiting their diagnosis and treatment (Ferreira, 2019).

claim: Knowledge of tissues and cell types that manifest with pathophysiological changes in patients facilitates the understanding of disease mechanisms.
source: Knowledge of tissues and cell types that manifest with pathophysiological changes in patients was shown to facilitate the understanding of disease mechanisms (Hekselman and Yeger-Lotem, 2020).

claim: Transcriptomic analysis of muscle tissues helped to genetically diagnose patients with rare muscle disorders.
source: For example, transcriptomic analysis of muscle tissues helped to genetically diagnose patients with rare muscle disorders (Cummings et al., 2017).

claim: Identification of a rare cell type affected by cystic fibrosis opened new avenues for treatment.
source: Likewise, identification of a rare cell type affected by cystic fibrosis opened new avenues for treatment (Montoro et al., 2018; Plasschaert et al., 2018).
evidence: Cited from Montoro et al., 2018 and Plasschaert et al., 2018

claim: The exact cell types that manifest with pathophysiological changes within affected tissues are often unknown for many Mendelian diseases.
source: However, whereas affected tissues may be evident for many Mendelian diseases, the exact cell types that manifest with pathophysiological changes within affected tissues are often unknown.
evidence: Statement based on the state of knowledge in the field

claim: Genes whose aberration leads to disease tend to be expressed preferentially in cell types that express pathology.
source: In particular, it was shown that genes whose aberration leads to disease (i.e., disease genes) tend to be expressed preferentially in cell types that express pathology (denoted disease-affected cell types).
evidence: General statement supported by subsequent examples and citations

claim: 21 out of 29 mouse homologs of human disease genes associated with nephrotic syndrome were upregulated in podocytes.
source: For instance, 21/29 mouse homologs of human disease genes associated with nephrotic syndrome were shown to be upregulated in podocytes, the disease-relevant renal cell type (Park et al., 2018).

claim: Podocytes are the disease-relevant renal cell type for nephrotic syndrome.
source: For instance, 21/29 mouse homologs of human disease genes associated with nephrotic syndrome were shown to be upregulated in podocytes, the disease-relevant renal cell type (Park et al., 2018).

claim: Cell-type-specific expression of the cystic fibrosis gene CFTR in ionocytes of human and mouse airways revealed their role in cystic fibrosis.
source: In an inspiring manner, cell-type-specific expression of the cystic fibrosis gene CFTR in ionocytes of human and mouse airways revealed their role in cystic fibrosis (Montoro et al., 2018; Plasschaert et al., 2018).
evidence: Cited from Montoro et al., 2018 and Plasschaert et al., 2018

claim: The preferential expression of disease genes for 18 Mendelian muscle disorders revealed disease-affected muscle cell types.
source: Likewise, the preferential expression of disease genes for 18 Mendelian muscle disorders revealed disease-affected muscle cell types (Eraslan et al., 2022).

claim: The study applied PrEDiCT to single-cell expression data of six human tissues.
source: We applied PrEDiCT to single-cell expression data of six human tissues, to infer the cell types affected in Mendelian diseases.

claim: The study inferred likely affected cell types for 328 diseases.
source: Overall, we inferred the likely affected cell types for 328 diseases.

claim: The study analyzed 1,140 Mendelian diseases that manifest in six human tissues.
source: We applied PrEDiCT to 1,140 Mendelian diseases that manifest in six human tissues and inferred likely affected cell types for 328 diseases.

claim: The six human tissues analyzed were bone marrow, lung, skeletal muscle, spleen, tongue and trachea.
source: Tissues included bone marrow, lung, skeletal muscle, spleen, tongue and trachea, and altogether were comprised of 129 cell types.

claim: The six tissues analyzed were comprised of 129 cell types.
source: Tissues included bone marrow, lung, skeletal muscle, spleen, tongue and trachea, and altogether were comprised of 129 cell types.

claim: The study identified 489 likely disease-cell-type associations.
source: We identified 489 (1.4%) 'likely' associations (PrEDiCT ≥ 1, FDR <0.1), covering 328/1140 diseases and 102/129 cell types.

claim: Likely associations covered 328 out of 1140 diseases.
source: We identified 489 (1.4%) 'likely' associations (PrEDiCT ≥ 1, FDR <0.1), covering 328/1140 diseases and 102/129 cell types.

claim: Likely associations covered 102 out of 129 cell types.
source: We identified 489 (1.4%) 'likely' associations (PrEDiCT ≥ 1, FDR <0.1), covering 328/1140 diseases and 102/129 cell types.

claim: Primary ciliary dyskinesia has 31 disease genes expressed in lung.
source: As proof-of-concept, primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD), which has 31 disease genes expressed in lung and is characterized by damaged ciliary machinery in lung ciliated cells (Leigh et al., 2019), was indeed likely associated with lung ciliated cells (Figure 1C).

claim: Primary ciliary dyskinesia is characterized by damaged ciliary machinery in lung ciliated cells.
source: As proof-of-concept, primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD), which has 31 disease genes expressed in lung and is characterized by damaged ciliary machinery in lung ciliated cells (Leigh et al., 2019), was indeed likely associated with lung ciliated cells (Figure 1C).

claim: Primary ciliary dyskinesia was likely associated with lung ciliated cells.
source: As proof-of-concept, primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD), which has 31 disease genes expressed in lung and is characterized by damaged ciliary machinery in lung ciliated cells (Leigh et al., 2019), was indeed likely associated with lung ciliated cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: Result from the study's analysis shown in Figure 1C

claim: Heinz body anemias is characterized by accumulation of inclusion bodies in erythrocytes.
source: Additionally, Heinz body anemias, which is characterized by accumulation of inclusion bodies in erythrocytes (Herman et al., 2023), was indeed likely associated with bone marrow erythrocytes (Figure 1D).

claim: Heinz body anemias was likely associated with bone marrow erythrocytes.
source: Additionally, Heinz body anemias, which is characterized by accumulation of inclusion bodies in erythrocytes (Herman et al., 2023), was indeed likely associated with bone marrow erythrocytes (Figure 1D).
evidence: Result from the study's analysis shown in Figure 1D

claim: Four out of five mitochondrial complex deficiencies were likely associated with slow and fast muscle cells.
source: Lastly, compatible with the high demand for mitochondrial activity in muscle cells, four out of five mitochondrial complex deficiencies were likely associated with slow and fast muscle cells (Figure 1E).
evidence: Result from the study's analysis shown in Figure 1E

claim: Mitochondrial complex II deficiency scored highest in slow and fast muscle cells but its PrEDiCT scores were insignificant.
source: 'Mitochondrial complex II deficiency' also scored highest in slow and fast muscle cells yet its PrEDiCT scores were insignificant, potentially due to the stringency of our statistical analysis (Figure 1E).
evidence: Result from the study's analysis shown in Figure 1E

claim: The study identified 229 literature-supported disease-cell-type pairs.
source: We identified 229 'literature-supported' pairs that co-appeared in the literature more often than expected by chance (adjusted p<0.001, Chi-squared test; Supplementary file 3).

claim: Likely disease-cell-type associations were enriched for literature supported pairs relative to all disease-cell-type associations.
source: Likely disease–cell-type associations were enriched for literature supported pairs (41/489, 8.4%) relative to all disease–cell-type associations (229/34,249, 0.7%; p<E-15, Fisher's exact test; Figure 1G).
evidence: Statistical analysis comparing likely associations to all associations

claim: The study analyzed 34,249 disease-cell-type associations in total.
source: In total, we analyzed 34,249 disease–cell-type associations (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Description of the study's analysis scope

claim: The study obtained 97 cell clusters across all six mouse tissues.
source: Altogether, we obtained 97 cell clusters across all six tissues (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Result from mouse single-cell data reanalysis

claim: The study identified 380 likely disease-cell-type associations in mouse.
source: The distribution of PrEDiCT scores was similar between mouse and human, and included 380/24,638 (1.5%) likely disease–cell-type associations (PrEDiCT ≥ 1, FDR < 0.1; Figure 2B; Supplementary file 6).

claim: PrEDiCT scores of matching cell types between human and mouse were modestly correlated.
source: Whereas PrEDiCT scores of non-matching cell types did not correlate (r=−0.02, Spearman correlation), PrEDiCT scores of matching types were modestly correlated (r=0.38, p<E-15, Spearman correlation; Figure 2F).
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis between human and mouse PrEDiCT scores

claim: PrEDiCT scores of non-matching cell types between human and mouse did not correlate.
source: Whereas PrEDiCT scores of non-matching cell types did not correlate (r=−0.02, Spearman correlation), PrEDiCT scores of matching types were modestly correlated (r=0.38, p<E-15, Spearman correlation; Figure 2F).
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis between human and mouse PrEDiCT scores

claim: 97 diseases (30% of 328 diseases with likely affected cell types in humans) affected matching cell types in mice.
source: Of the 328 diseases with likely affected cell types in humans, 97 diseases (30%) affected matching cell types in mice, a fraction that was larger than expected by chance (adjusted p<0.01, permutation test; Figure 2G and Supplementary file 6; Methods).
evidence: Result from comparison between human and mouse analyses

claim: The fraction of diseases affecting matching cell types in mice was larger than expected by chance.
source: Of the 328 diseases with likely affected cell types in humans, 97 diseases (30%) affected matching cell types in mice, a fraction that was larger than expected by chance (adjusted p<0.01, permutation test; Figure 2G and Supplementary file 6; Methods).

claim: Most diseases with a likely affected cell type manifested clinically in two or more tissues.
source: Most diseases with a likely affected cell type manifested clinically in two or more tissues, and were denoted multi-tissue diseases (168/328, 51%; Figure 3A).

claim: 168 out of 328 diseases with a likely affected cell type were multi-tissue diseases.
source: Most diseases with a likely affected cell type manifested clinically in two or more tissues, and were denoted multi-tissue diseases (168/328, 51%; Figure 3A).

claim: The study identified 840 pairs of matching cell types between tissues.
source: Overall, we identified 840 pairs of matching cell types between tissues, of which 52% were immunocytes, including macrophages, neutrophils, T cells, B cells, as well as endothelia and fibroblasts.
evidence: Result from cell type matching analysis

claim: 52% of matching cell type pairs between tissues were immunocytes.
source: Overall, we identified 840 pairs of matching cell types between tissues, of which 52% were immunocytes, including macrophages, neutrophils, T cells, B cells, as well as endothelia and fibroblasts.
evidence: Result from cell type matching analysis

claim: 18% of multi-tissue diseases likely affected at least one pair of matching cell types.
source: We found that 18% (30/168) of the diseases likely affected at least one pair of matching cell types, a fraction higher than expected by chance (adjusted p<0.01, permutation test; Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Methods).

claim: The fraction of diseases affecting matching cell types between tissues was higher than expected by chance.
source: We found that 18% (30/168) of the diseases likely affected at least one pair of matching cell types, a fraction higher than expected by chance (adjusted p<0.01, permutation test; Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Methods).

claim: Chronic granulomatous disease results in splenomegaly and pneumonia due to impaired phagocytes.
source: For instance, chronic granulomatous disease (CGD) results in splenomegaly and pneumonia due to impaired phagocytes (i.e., neutrophils, macrophages, and monocytes; Anjani et al., 2020; Leiding and Holland, 1993).
evidence: Cited from Anjani et al., 2020 and Leiding and Holland, 1993

claim: Neutrophils, macrophages, and monocytes were the likely affected cell types for chronic granulomatous disease in both spleen and lung.
source: These cell types were indeed the likely affected cell types for CGD in both spleen and lung (Figure 3C).
evidence: Result from the study's analysis shown in Figure 3C

claim: Chronic granulomatous disease likely affected bone-marrow phagocytes.
source: Also, CGD likely affected bone-marrow phagocytes, consistent with bone-marrow transplant being a curative treatment for this disease (Leiding and Holland, 1993).
evidence: Result from the study's analysis and cited from Leiding and Holland, 1993

claim: Bone-marrow transplant is a curative treatment for chronic granulomatous disease.
source: Also, CGD likely affected bone-marrow phagocytes, consistent with bone-marrow transplant being a curative treatment for this disease (Leiding and Holland, 1993).

claim: Hyper-IgM immunodeficiency could arise from mutations in CD40 gene, affecting B cells, or mutations in CD40 ligand (CD40LG), affecting CD4 T cells.
source: For example, the bone-marrow disease hyper-IgM immunodeficiency could arise from mutations in CD40 gene, affecting B cells, or mutations in CD40 ligand (CD40LG), affecting CD4 T cells (Yazdani et al., 2019).

claim: Only CD4 T cells were predicted as likely affected by hyper-IgM immunodeficiency when applying PrEDiCT to all disease genes jointly.
source: Indeed, only CD4 T cells were predicted as likely affected by hyper-IgM immunodeficiency (PrEDiCT = 1.6, FDR <0.048).

claim: Hyper-IgM immunodeficiency was found to likely affect naïve B cells through CD40 (receptor).
source: As expected, hyper-IgM immunodeficiency was found to likely affect naïve B cells through CD40 (receptor; PrEDiCT = 2.9, FDR = 0.06), and CD4αβ T cells through CD40LG (ligand; PrEDiCT = 3.7, FDR <0.001; Figure 4A).
evidence: Result from separate analysis of ligands and receptors

claim: Hyper-IgM immunodeficiency was found to likely affect CD4αβ T cells through CD40LG (ligand).
source: As expected, hyper-IgM immunodeficiency was found to likely affect naïve B cells through CD40 (receptor; PrEDiCT = 2.9, FDR = 0.06), and CD4αβ T cells through CD40LG (ligand; PrEDiCT = 3.7, FDR <0.001; Figure 4A).
evidence: Result from separate analysis of ligands and receptors

claim: Autosomal recessive limb-girdle muscular dystrophy is caused by mutations in laminin-α2 (LAMA2) or its receptor α-dystroglycan (DAG1).
source: Another example is autosomal recessive limb-girdle muscular dystrophy, which is caused by mutations in laminin-α2 (LAMA2) or its receptor α-dystroglycan (DAG1).

claim: By separately applying PrEDiCT scheme to LAMA2 (ligand) and DAG1 (receptor), mesenchymal stem cells and satellite stem cells were inferred as the likely affected cell types for autosomal recessive limb-girdle muscular dystrophy, respectively.
source: Yet, by separately applying PrEDiCT scheme to LAMA2 (ligand) and DAG1 (receptor), we inferred mesenchymal stem cells and satellite stem cells as the likely affected cell types, respectively (PrEDiCT = 3.8 and 3.7, FDR <0.05; Figure 4B).
evidence: Result from separate analysis of ligands and receptors

claim: Disruption of DAG1 in satellite stem cells has been associated with the defective muscle regeneration seen in diseased patients with autosomal recessive limb-girdle muscular dystrophy.
source: In support of the prediction for DAG1, disruption of DAG1 in satellite stem cells has been associated with the defective muscle regeneration seen in diseased patients (Cohn et al., 2002; Servián-Morilla et al., 2020).
evidence: Cited from Cohn et al., 2002 and Servián-Morilla et al., 2020

claim: Autosomal recessive limb-girdle muscular dystrophy was attenuated in ligand-knockout [Col6a1(-/-)] model mice by supplying wild-type mesenchymal-stem-cell derived fibroblasts.
source: In support of the prediction for LAMA2, the disease was attenuated in ligand-knockout [Col6a1(-/-)] model mice by supplying wild-type mesenchymal-stem-cell derived fibroblasts.

claim: Treatment with wild-type mesenchymal-stem-cell derived fibroblasts not only restored the collagen VI of the tissue, but also rescued defects in satellite stem cells in ligand-knockout model mice.
source: This treatment not only restored the collagen VI of the tissue, but also rescued defects in satellite stem cells (Urciuolo et al., 2013).

claim: In airway cancers, the joint application of PrEDiCT scheme inferred both basal cells and intermediate monocytes as likely affected.
source: For example, in airway cancers (lung and trachea), the joint application of PrEDiCT scheme inferred both basal cells and intermediate monocytes as likely affected.

claim: In airway cancers, the separate application of PrEDiCT inferred basal cells as likely affected by oncogenes, and intermediate and non-classical monocytes as likely affected by TSGs.
source: The separate application inferred basal cells as likely affected by oncogenes, and intermediate and non-classical monocytes as likely affected by TSGs (Figure 4C).
evidence: Result from separate analysis of oncogenes and TSGs

claim: Capillary endothelial cells of the tongue were the most susceptible cell type.
source: Most susceptible were capillary endothelial cells of the tongue (Susceptibility = 25%; Figure 5A), which were affected by diseases that result in morphologic aberrations of the tongue (e.g., telangiectasia and macroglossia).

claim: Capillary endothelial cells of the tongue were affected by diseases that result in morphologic aberrations of the tongue.
source: Most susceptible were capillary endothelial cells of the tongue (Susceptibility = 25%; Figure 5A), which were affected by diseases that result in morphologic aberrations of the tongue (e.g., telangiectasia and macroglossia).

claim: Cell-type susceptibility did not correlate with cell-type prevalence.
source: The two measures did not correlate (r=−0.02, Pearson correlation; Figure 5A).

claim: Fast and slow muscle cells were the most susceptible cell types in skeletal muscle.
source: For example, fast and slow muscle cells were the most susceptible cell types in skeletal muscle, while each accounting for less than 1% of the cells in that tissue.

claim: Fast and slow muscle cells each accounted for less than 1% of the cells in skeletal muscle tissue.
source: For example, fast and slow muscle cells were the most susceptible cell types in skeletal muscle, while each accounting for less than 1% of the cells in that tissue.

claim: Cell-type susceptibility varied between cell classes.
source: Cell classes had varying susceptibility (Figure 5B; p=1.5E-3, ANOVA).

claim: Among common cell classes, immunocytes and epithelia were the least susceptible.
source: Among the common cell classes, immunocytes and epithelia were the least susceptible, and endothelia were the most susceptible compared to other cell types (adjusted p<0.05, Mann-Whitney U test; Methods).

claim: Among common cell classes, endothelia were the most susceptible compared to other cell types.
source: Among the common cell classes, immunocytes and epithelia were the least susceptible, and endothelia were the most susceptible compared to other cell types (adjusted p<0.05, Mann-Whitney U test; Methods).

claim: HPO annotations asserted 490 of 649 (76%) annotations available for these diseases in ODiseA.
source: This asserted 490 of 649 (76%) annotations available for these diseases in ODiseA, supporting the usage of HPO as an indicator of the disease-affected tissue.
evidence: Comparison between HPO and ODiseA annotations

claim: 1140 diseases and 2434 disease genes were associated to at least one affected tissue.
source: Overall, 1140 diseases and 2434 disease genes were associated to at least one affected tissue, with the majority associated to skeletal muscle (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1).

claim: The majority of diseases were associated to skeletal muscle.
source: Overall, 1140 diseases and 2434 disease genes were associated to at least one affected tissue, with the majority associated to skeletal muscle (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1).

claim: The PrEDiCT score of a disease in each cell type was set to the median preferential expression of the respective disease genes.
source: Next, we set the PrEDiCT score of a disease in each cell type to the median preferential expression of the respective disease genes.

claim: Statistical significance of the PrEDiCT score was determined using a permutation test.
source: Statistical significance of the score was determined using a permutation test (Methods; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).

claim: The false-positive rates for likely associations were low.
source: The false-positive rates for likely associations were low (Methods; Figure 1F).

claim: A large variety of human cell types had a matching mouse cell type (82/129).
source: As expected, a large variety of human cell types had a matching mouse cell type (82/129) and vice versa (70/97; Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Result from cell type matching analysis

claim: 70 out of 97 mouse cell types had a matching human cell type.
source: As expected, a large variety of human cell types had a matching mouse cell type (82/129) and vice versa (70/97; Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Result from cell type matching analysis

claim: The impact of disease genes on the matching between human and mouse cell types was negligible.
source: The impact of disease genes on the matching was negligible, as shown by repeating the identification of similar cell types upon excluding disease genes from the list of marker genes (Methods).

claim: Primary ciliary dyskinesia likely affected mouse lung ciliated epithelial cells which match human lung ciliated cells.
source: Compatible with our previous proof-of-concept cases in human, PCD likely affected mouse lung ciliated epithelial cells which match human lung ciliated cells (Figure 2C), and Heinz body anemias likely affected mouse bone marrow reticulocytes and erythroblasts which match human erythrocytes (Figure 2D).
evidence: Result from mouse analysis shown in Figure 2C

claim: Heinz body anemias likely affected mouse bone marrow reticulocytes and erythroblasts which match human erythrocytes.
source: Compatible with our previous proof-of-concept cases in human, PCD likely affected mouse lung ciliated epithelial cells which match human lung ciliated cells (Figure 2C), and Heinz body anemias likely affected mouse bone marrow reticulocytes and erythroblasts which match human erythrocytes (Figure 2D).
evidence: Result from mouse analysis shown in Figure 2D

claim: Four mitochondrial complex deficiencies likely affected mouse striated muscle cells, which matched human slow and fast muscle cells.
source: Likewise, four mitochondrial complex deficiencies likely affected mouse striated muscle cells, which matched human slow and fast muscle cells (Figure 2E).
evidence: Result from mouse analysis shown in Figure 2E

claim: Mitochondrial complex II deficiency scored highest in mouse striated muscle cells, yet the scores were insignificant.
source: Similar to the results in human, 'mitochondrial complex II deficiency' scored highest in these cell types, yet the scores were insignificant (Figure 2E).
evidence: Result from mouse analysis shown in Figure 2E

claim: The study identified seven diseases in the dataset that were caused by mutations in genes encoding ligands and their receptors.
source: We identified seven diseases in our dataset that were caused by mutations in genes encoding ligands and their receptors.

claim: About 30% of Mendelian diseases manifest clinically in a tissue that overexpresses disease genes.
source: Interestingly, this fits with previous observations that about 30% of Mendelian diseases manifest clinically in a tissue that overexpresses disease genes (Barshir et al., 2018; Barshir et al., 2014; Hekselman and Yeger-Lotem, 2020; Lage et al., 2008).
evidence: Cited from Barshir et al., 2018; Barshir et al., 2014; Hekselman and Yeger-Lotem, 2020; Lage et al., 2008

claim: The fraction of associations that were recapitulated in mouse did not differ between diseases with a single or multiple disease genes.
source: However, the fraction of associations that were recapitulated in mouse did not differ between diseases with a single or multiple disease genes, supporting this line of evidence (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Result from comparison analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: 328 diseases affected 102 out of 129 cell types.
source: Overall, 328 diseases affected 102/129 cell types.

claim: There was no correlation between cell type prevalence and its likelihood to be affected.
source: Interestingly, there was no correlation between cell type prevalence and its likelihood to be affected (Figure 5A).
evidence: Result from correlation analysis shown in Figure 5A

claim: Endothelia were more likely to be affected by diseases than other prevalent cell classes.
source: In particular, endothelia were more likely to be affected by diseases than other prevalent cell classes, whereas immunocytes and epithelia were the least likely to be affected among the prevalent cell classes (Figure 5B).
evidence: Result from susceptibility analysis shown in Figure 5B

claim: Immunocytes had similar expression signatures across tissues, in accordance with their common functions.
source: To analyze this further, a cross-tissue study of 20 human tissues showed that immunocytes had similar expression signatures across tissues, in accordance with their common functions, whereas endothelia had tissue-specific expression signatures that reflect their tissue-specialized roles (Jones et al., 2022).

claim: Endothelia had tissue-specific expression signatures that reflect their tissue-specialized roles.
source: To analyze this further, a cross-tissue study of 20 human tissues showed that immunocytes had similar expression signatures across tissues, in accordance with their common functions, whereas endothelia had tissue-specific expression signatures that reflect their tissue-specialized roles (Jones et al., 2022).

claim: Germline impairment of immunocytes is more likely lethal.
source: Hence, it seems that germline impairment of immunocytes is more likely lethal, whereas the tissue-specialization of endothelia limits the impact of their germline impairment and thus facilitates overall survival.
evidence: Inference based on expression signature data and susceptibility patterns

claim: The tissue-specialization of endothelia limits the impact of their germline impairment and thus facilitates overall survival.
source: Hence, it seems that germline impairment of immunocytes is more likely lethal, whereas the tissue-specialization of endothelia limits the impact of their germline impairment and thus facilitates overall survival.

claim: Mitochondrial diseases tend to affect muscle cells, in accordance with their energetic demands.
source: For example, we showed that mitochondrial diseases tend to affect muscle cells, in accordance with their energetic demands (Figure 1E).

claim: Diseases inflicting on multiple tissues likely affect similar cell types among those tissues.
source: Additionally, we showed that diseases inflicting on multiple tissues likely affect similar cell types among those tissues, thereby providing a mechanistic explanation for this phenomenon (Figure 3).

claim: Oncogenes of heritable lung and trachea cancers likely affect basal cells.
source: For instance, by separately analyzing oncogenes and TSGs of heritable lung and trachea cancers, we found that oncogenes likely affect basal cells, and TSGs likely affect monocytes (Figure 4C).

claim: TSGs of heritable lung and trachea cancers likely affect monocytes.
source: For instance, by separately analyzing oncogenes and TSGs of heritable lung and trachea cancers, we found that oncogenes likely affect basal cells, and TSGs likely affect monocytes (Figure 4C).
evidence: Result from separate analysis shown in Figure 4C

claim: Tissue-constructive cells are more susceptible to oncogene mutations.
source: This could suggest that tissue-constructive cells are more susceptible to oncogene mutations, whereas protective cells, such as monocytes, are more susceptible to TSG mutations.

claim: Protective cells, such as monocytes, are more susceptible to TSG mutations.
source: This could suggest that tissue-constructive cells are more susceptible to oncogene mutations, whereas protective cells, such as monocytes, are more susceptible to TSG mutations.

claim: Monocytes function in the elimination of malignant transformation of cells in different tissues.
source: The latter is consistent with the function of monocytes in the elimination of malignant transformation of cells in different tissues (Robinson et al., 2021).

claim: Autosomal recessive limb-girdle muscular dystrophy disrupts intercellular communication among muscle cell types, via mutations in the DAG1 receptor.
source: Consistent with their results, we found that autosomal recessive limb-girdle muscular dystrophy disrupts intercellular communication among muscle cell types, via mutations in the DAG1 receptor (Figure 4B).

claim: By applying PrEDiCT separately to the ligand of DAG1, LAMA2, the study highlighted the involvement of mesenchymal stem cells in autosomal recessive limb-girdle muscular dystrophy.
source: Yet, by applying PrEDiCT separately to the ligand of DAG1, LAMA2, we also highlighted the involvement of mesenchymal stem cells in the disease (Urciuolo et al., 2013).
